newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to support ailing financial institutions.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to support ailing financial institutions.

text.p: South Korea's Finance Ministry said on Monday it would help finance troubled financial institutions on condition that they submit satisfactory self-rescue programmes.
A ministry statement said state-run Korea Asset Management Corp would extend aid by buying some assets held by ailing financial institutions to help ease their credit constraints.
But funds would be provided only when the financial companies submitted restructuring plans deemed acceptable by the government and the central bank.
The Korea Asset Management Corp, set up in 1962, is the state-owned liquidation company.
The corporation collects overdue loans, sells off real estate on behalf of financial institutions and arranges public auctions of state property.
The ministry statement said the government would allow the corporation to raise its funding from the current 1.5 trillion won to an amount not yet determined.
To increase its funding, the corporation would borrow low-interest loans from the central bank and issue long-term bonds.

The ministry statement said the decision was made in a meeting on Saturday between Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik, central bank governor Lee Kyung-shick and Kim In-ho, chief economic adviser to President Kim Young-sam.
The statement said the government needed to supply "minimum supports" so that financial institutions could normalise their operations on their own.
Liquidity problems in South Korea's financial industry surfaced after Korea First Bank asked the central bank for special loans of three trillion won.
The bank was hit hard by a chain of corporate defaults including the collapse of Hanbo Steel and Sammi Steel.
It is now facing another possible big blow by troubled Kia Group, which was put under its creditors' protection in July.
The statement said the government and the central bank had agreed in principle that Korea First would be the first financial institution to receive money from the Korea Asset Management Corp.

Korea First is scheduled to submit more detailed self-rescue measures to the finance ministry and central bank on Saturday. It remains unclear whether the central bank would extend special loans to Korea First.
"Given the significance of such loans, special loans from the central bank would be granted only if it were really urgent," a ministry official said.
The official said one concern about such loans would be the increase in money supply that would result.
